location: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — Fiberglass Bust of Benjamin Franklin

location: Lake Champlain, New York–Vermont — New Bridge
recipient: Mr. Joseph R. Page, Greene, New York
notes: Postmarked Colebrook, NH, Jul 22, 1937, 10 AM. 1¢ Franklin stamp. C.T. Art-Colortone Reg. U.S. Pat. Off., Made only by Curt Teich & Co., Inc., Chicago. Fairchild Aerial Surveys, Inc., N.Y.C. Card 5A-H175. Caption: ‘New Bridge Across Lake Champlain Uniting the States of New York and Vermont.’ Front shows an aerial view of the new steel arch bridge spanning Lake Champlain with rolling green farmland on both shores. Message: “Dear [?] + Lymans. [Arrived] Tuesday after noon and had a delightful day. Picnic and [stayed] at Rouses Point for the night. Crossed the new bridge this a.m. and down Lake Champlain to Burlington, Montpelier, Barnes and now here at Miriam Farm, a place for tourists. It has been a fine day — many lakes and through woods and an old covered bridge. The mountains are great. We have had nice miniature [?] had lunch at a camp and [got shady?] was tired. On to Bangor. If you care back to the Burwells. With love to both. Aunt Sandy.”

location: Staten Island, New York — Fort Wadsworth
recipient: Mr. & Mrs. Harry, P.O. Box 503, Lisco, Nebraska

I must bid you a cheerio good night and may God bless you one and all mother and dad, I still remain as ever Freddie.”

location: Northern Ontario, Canada — Scenic Multiview
recipient: Hillary Harrow, 401 S. Camden Dr. #6, Beverly Hills, California 90212
notes: Postmarked 1988 (Sault Ste. Marie area). 25¢ Jack London stamp + $0.29 meter. Published by Soo Photo Service Ltd., Canadian Photoscene Products Inc., Sault Ste. Marie, Ont. Card No. 36390-D. Us & I never really said ‘goodbye’ on Saturday — that’s weird. She & Matt were together the whole last couple of days. I feel bad, but there’s nothing to be done, I s’pose. I see Mitch on Friday! God — how exciting! Then, I’ll vege some next week & start my job on next Fri. on the Island! HOO-RAY! I have this urge to be in Beantown badly — but not w/out you! Slut! Will it be any fun when I visit Lis at Hah-vahd? I need Newbury Street & Davis’s!! I’ll probably end up going to BU anyway — & you? ♡ G—” Grad. was nice & up-lifting! VIP-EEE! I ♡ North Ontario.

location: Houston, Texas — “Fire Scene on Main Street” (comic novelty)

notes: No postmark. No stamp affixed — stamp box reads ‘Place Stamp Here / Domestic One Cent / Foreign Two Cents,’ indicating early divided-back era (post-1907). Card format and printing style suggest c. 1905–1910. No recipient address given beyond name. Undivided address side. Published by unknown (card number 205 lower right). Front is a chromolithograph comic novelty card — a busy rural scene satirizing small-town Texas life: a two-story wooden Post Office building at center with a figure in the doorway, a locomotive warning sign reading ‘Look Out for the Train!! On Tuesdays,’ a cow poking its head through a fence at left, a sow with piglets in a mud puddle, a hen with chicks in the foreground, and a barn fully ablaze in the background. The caption reads ‘Houston, Texas — Fire Scene on Main Street’ in red type. Message from Walter to his brother T.J. Nelson: “their has been three big fires on mainst in the last 4 months the bigest a hole flock burned out facing main st. the first one goodby answer soon your Brother walter.” The misspellings (‘their’ for ‘there,’ ‘bigest,’ ‘a hole flock’ for ‘a whole block’) are phonetic and characteristic of vernacular early-20th-century correspondence. The comic front image — depicting fires as a rural joke — takes on an eerie resonance given Walter’s actual report of three downtown fires.

location: Bethlehem, Pennsylvania — Easter Greeting

Titled ‘Köln am Rhein/Cologne — Dom in Festbeleuchtung / Cathedral — Festive panorama.’ A striking nighttime aerial shot of the Kölner Dom bathed in green floodlights, the twin Gothic spires dominating the skyline above the Rhine riverfront. The Colonius telecommunications tower visible to the left. Sally is writing to her parents (the McLoutits) from an independent European tour with travel companion David, having arrived via Amsterdam. She mentions a 9-hour train ride from Amsterdam, jet lag, dragging a wheeled suitcase, sitting by the Rhine in evening light, church bells ringing, and James in the background. A warm, detailed window into independent European travel in 1993. Note: Mary McLouth (Tyler, TX) is believed to be a relative of the Wickenburg McLoutit family — both appear as recipients in the archive. Message: “Dearest Mom & Dad — All is well! Cologne is more beautiful & different than Netherlands. David is very organized and never runs out of energy or patience for touring or me. We start on the tour tomorrow. It is warm not hot — we are sitting on the lawn you see in the postcard by the water except it is light — the church bells ring and a youthful happy James is on the horn in the background. We had a 9-hour train ride yesterday from Amsterdam. Jet lag took most of Day 2 of our trip. No trouble finding reasonable places to stay. We push or pull or drag our suitcase on wheels every place. Hope all is well for you. Call Lisa or Ted when you get lonesome and check on Ben. Love you, Sally. July 23.”

location: Bochum, Germany — Schauspielhaus (Municipal Theatre)
year: c. mid-to-late 1950s (postmark day legible, year worn away — see notes)
recipient: Mrs. Elisabeth Pfanneberg, c/o Mimno, 83 Pleasant Street, Lexington 73, Massachusetts, USA
notes: Published by Verlag Heinr. Koch, Essen (card 56272). Black-and-white real-photo card of Bochum's Schauspielhaus (municipal drama theatre) seen across its landscaped park grounds, benches and flowering shrubs in the foreground. Sent airmail (“Mit Luftpost / Par Avion” label) with a 40pf blue Theodor Heuss definitive stamp (West German series issued 1954–1960). Postmark shows a Bochum-area cancellation dated the 31st of May, but the year digit isn’t legible on the scan. Addressed to “Lexington 73” — a pre-ZIP postal zone number (zones were retired when ZIP codes launched in 1963), which narrows the likely date to sometime before then, consistent with the Heuss stamp’s 1954–1960 run. Ballparking it to the mid-to-late 1950s on that basis. Message is written in fast, looping German cursive (closer to old Kurrentschrift style than modern hand) across the full back and margin. Best-effort reading after close inspection: opens with “Liebe Mutti!” (“Dear Mommy!”); the body’s content resists confident word-for-word transcription, but its tone reads as warm, casual family chat — touching on good weather/sunshine and day-to-day activities rather than any specific news. It closes with a “viele liebe Grüße” (“many warm greetings”) sign-off signed by several family members, including what appears to be “Oma” (Grandma) — suggesting a multi-generational family greeting rather than a single letter-writer. Sent to Elisabeth Pfanneberg, care of a “Mimno” household in Lexington, Massachusetts — likely German relatives writing to family who had emigrated to the Boston area. Note: the message body remains only partially deciphered despite repeated close review; a native reader of old German cursive would likely get more out of it than this transcription does.

location: Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — Candelária Church

recipient: Mr. & Mrs. Felix Yoder, Berne, Ind.

location: Allenstein, East Prussia (now Olsztyn, Poland) — Castle
recipient: Frau Martha [surname illegible], Berlin, Germany
notes: Front caption: “Allenstein. Partie am Schloß” — a hand-tinted photo of Allenstein Castle's distinctive red tower and Gothic brick hall beside a tree-lined canal. The castle is a 14th-century Teutonic Order stronghold (Ordensburg), begun around 1347–53 as the administrative seat of the Warmia cathedral chapter. Its most famous resident was the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, who lived here as chapter administrator from 1516–1521 and personally organized the town's successful defense during a Teutonic Knights' siege in 1520–21. Allenstein was German territory (East Prussia) when this card was sent; after WWII it was transferred to Poland and renamed Olsztyn, its German population expelled in 1945. This is a Feldpost (military field-post) card, exempt from postage under wartime rules, postmarked Allenstein, 13 October 1917 — deep in WWI, about a year before the Armistice. The address and message are both written sideways, running up the card rather than across. Address (partially legible): “Feldpost. Frau Martha [surname illegible], Berlin,” with what may be an old Berlin postal-district code alongside it. The message, in dense wartime cursive, opens “Liebe Frau!” (“Dear wife!” or “Dear Mrs. [name]!”) and seems to touch on travel and field-post/airmail arrangements, but honestly resisted a confident line-by-line transcription even after repeated review — the handwriting leans on a heavily abbreviated, period Kurrentschrift-influenced style. It's signed by several names at the bottom, including what looks like a cavalry rank abbreviation (“Ulan.”, short for Ulanen — lancer cavalry) followed by names including “P. Kaatz” and “Paul Nasser,” with at least one more only partly legible — suggesting a joint greeting from a group of soldier comrades to one of their wives back home. Flagging the body of this one honestly as only partially deciphered; a reader fluent in old German military cursive would likely get more out of it.

location: Salt Lake City, Utah — Brigham Young's Grave
address: Brigham Young Family Cemetery, 140 East 1st Avenue, Salt Lake City, UT
recipient: Mrs. Viola Berry[?] (surname could also read “Berney”), Breckenridge P.O., Caldwell Co., Missouri
notes: Front: “1003. Brigham Young's Grave, Salt Lake City, Utah” — a tinted photo of the ornate wrought-iron-fenced tomb of Brigham Young (1801–1877), second president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, who led the Mormon pioneers into the Salt Lake Valley in 1847 and served as the first governor of Utah Territory. He's buried in a small private family cemetery just northeast of Temple Square, alongside other family members and early Church figures. Back: published by The Thayer Publishing Co., Denver, Colo., with the printed reassurance “THIS SPACE CAN BE USED FOR A WRITTEN MESSAGE, USING ONE-CENT STAMP” — the kind of note publishers commonly added right after the U.S. Post Office's March 1907 rule change permitting a divided back (message and address sharing one side). Paired with the 1-cent green Franklin stamp of that same general era, this points to a card from roughly 1907 into the early 1910s, though the postmark itself is too worn to confirm an exact year. Message: “Well how are you. I am at Depot at Salt Lake. am well had to-Lay over Train. Late Every thing shut down in my Business. if I can't get to business in Colorado will be home soon. Your as Ever R H Berry” — the writer delayed en route on a train layover, business plans up in the air. Addressed to “Mrs. Viola Berry” (the surname could also be read as “Berney” — genuinely hard to resolve, though “Berry” would match the sender's own signature), “Breckenridge P.O., Caldwell Co., Mo.” — Breckenridge is a real small town in Caldwell County already familiar from a couple of other cards in the archive.

location: Trappenkamp, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany
recipient: Herrn Albert Hueske, 509 Ave of Oaks, Houston, Tex. 77009, U.S.A.
notes: This card came in filed as “Unknown” — the front carries no printed caption — but the return address on the back gives it away: this is Trappenkamp itself. The aerial front photo shows a purpose-built settlement of identical red-roofed apartment blocks laid out along straight streets, ringed by heathland and forest with dunes and open water visible in the distance. Trappenkamp has a striking origin story: the town didn't exist before the 1930s. The site began as “Gönnebeker Heide,” a Prussian cavalry and infantry parade ground; in July 1934 the German Navy chose the site (by then state forest) to build a mine-storage depot relieving pressure on the naval arsenal at Kiel. British troops occupied it on 18 May 1945, and afterward it was repurposed as a refugee camp for Germans expelled from the eastern territories and the Sudetenland. It became its own independent municipality in April 1956, having previously been administered as part of neighboring Bornhöved. The front photo captures exactly this transformation — a former military depot reborn as row after row of refugee housing. The return address, written by the sender at the top of the card per German convention, reads “2351 Trappenkamp / Arndtstr. 31” — “2351” is an old West German four-digit postal code, consistent with a mid-20th-century date. A printed clearance code at the bottom, “Frei. Reg. Präs. Düss. 17-C 208,” is the kind of official image-rights approval stamp West German postcard publishers commonly carried at the time. Message (German): “Unser lieber Vetter Albert! Gottes Segen für Dein neues Lebensjahr, viel Glück, Freude u. Gesundheit für Dich u. Hildegard. Wo das X auf der Karte, in der Richtung wohnen wir. Viel schöne Stunden wünschen Euch in Liebe Eure Werner u. Hemchen.” Translation: “Our dear cousin Albert! God's blessing for your new year of life [i.e. happy birthday], much luck, joy and health for you and Hildegard. Where the X is on the card, that's the direction we live in. Wishing you many lovely hours, with love, your Werner and Hemchen.” Addressed to Albert Hueske at 509 Ave of Oaks, Houston, Texas — the very same street address as the Brauer family's Laredo postcard already in the archive (card #184) — very likely the same household or a close relative, both maintaining ties with German family back home. Worth a look for the Family Networks tag.

notes: Printed QSL card, red block lettering ‘W7RT.’ Confirms: WITH KL7BE, ON Apr. 25 1949, BAND 3.5mc Fone. UR SIGS: (5)9-FB! RMX: ‘Tks QSO — Using 9 watts. Input 6V6 final BC-474 portable here — Hi Rx HRO+.’ OLD K7RT (Goodnews Bay, Alaska). Signed John Gruble, Ex-SCM, ARRL, RSGB, NZART, WIA (‘Over 10,000 contacts since 1929, all bands’). Handwritten note on back, same sender. Message: “This little Rig, one of several portables, will be using during Field Day Test June 18–19 — Have 500W AC gas plant on 2-wheel trailer. Regular xmtr's 300W to PP 811's. 73, John, W7RT. Pse QSL enclosed card & business card to KL7AH & thanks OM!”

recipient: Mrs. J.A. Murray, Cambridge Springs, R.D. #3, Pennsylvania
notes: Front: sepia real-photo postcard of a young bear cub among tall pines, captioned in white ink ‘A Canyon Baby’ with a photographer/studio credit below that’s not fully legible [best guess: something like ‘Caukins’]. 2¢ John Adams stamp. Message: “Tues. Dear Florence, We just received a card D. They are coming up this week, so I don't know what to tell you about Sun. We were planning to come until the card came. I think it will be better to wait until later to come. Sorry! But think that will be best.”
